title: Huguenots
capsule: During 1622–1632 the Huguenots functioned as a quasi-state within France: under the Edict of Nantes (1598) they controlled some 66 fortified towns (villes de sûreté), maintained independent armies, and conducted foreign diplomacy. Three successive Huguenot wars against the Crown (1621–1629) ended with the Peace of Alès in 1629, by which Cardinal Richelieu stripped them of all political and military privileges—most critically after the royal siege and capitulation of La Rochelle in October 1628—while nominally preserving their right of worship. The residual period to 1632 reflects the final suppression of armed resistance in the south before the Edict of Grace of Alès was fully enforced.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Huguenot 'state within a state' had documented territorial control of specific fortified towns, but the geographic footprint was fragmented and shifted rapidly with each siege; the extent shown in any single year is necessarily approximate.
